definition: Anomaly Detection at Multiple Scales, or ADAMS was a $35 million DARPA project designed to identify patterns and anomalies in very large data sets.
details: It is under DARPA's Information Innovation office and began in 2011 and ended in August 2014 The project was intended to detect and prevent insider threats such as "a soldier in good mental health becoming homicidal or suicidal", an "innocent insider becoming malicious", or "a government employee [who] abuses access privileges to share classified information". Specific cases mentioned are Nadal Malik Hasan and WikiLeaks source Chelsea Manning. Commercial applications may include finance. The intended recipients of the system output are operators in the counterintelligence agencies. A final report was published on May 11, 2015, detailing a system known as Anomaly Detection Engine for Networks, or ADEN, developed by the University of Maryland, College Park, whose goal was to "identify malicious users within a network." Using multiple datasets from Wikipedia, Slashdot, and others, researchers were able to identify vandals and malicious users on a website using both conventional algorithms and artificial intelligence. explainer.lead: ADAMS was a $35 million DARPA project that looked for unusual patterns in very large datasets, with the aim of detecting insider threats before they caused harm. Its work included ADEN, a system demonstrated on online-community data to identify vandals and malicious users.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a school keeping millions of notes about what happens in its hallways. Most notes describe ordinary behaviour, but a strange pattern could warn a helper that someone is breaking important rules. ADAMS tried to build computer systems that could find those warning patterns in enormous collections of information.
tiers.practitioner: Treat ADAMS as a research programme rather than an off-the-shelf detector: the described workflow applies conventional algorithms and artificial intelligence to large activity datasets, then supplies findings to counterintelligence operators. ADEN was evaluated with datasets from Wikipedia, Slashdot and others to identify vandals and malicious users. A practical pitfall is expecting a specified model, feature set or threshold from the ADAMS name; the programme encompassed multiple research efforts.
tiers.paperLevel: ADAMS addressed anomaly detection over very large datasets, with the application objective of identifying behavioural patterns associated with insider threats. It ran under DARPA's Information Innovation office from 2011 to August 2014 and included Proactive Discovery of Insider Threats Using Graph Analysis and Learning. Its final report, published on May 11, 2015, described the University of Maryland, College Park system ADEN, whose objective was to identify malicious users within a network; no single formal model or scoring function defines the programme.

explainer.example: In the ADEN work reported on May 11, 2015, University of Maryland, College Park researchers used datasets from Wikipedia, Slashdot and other sites. By applying conventional algorithms and artificial intelligence, they identified vandals and malicious users, illustrating ADAMS's broader goal of finding harmful insiders within a network.

explainer.intuition: Harmful insiders can be difficult to spot when their actions are buried among huge volumes of normal activity. ADAMS sought computational ways to find suspicious patterns and anomalies, including cases where an apparently trustworthy person became malicious or abused access to classified information.
howItWorks: Bring together very large datasets containing relevant activity.
Analyse the data with conventional algorithms and artificial intelligence to find patterns and anomalies.
Use those findings to flag potentially malicious users or insider-threat behaviour.
Deliver the system's output to counterintelligence operators.
explainer.whyItMatters: The project addressed threats that ordinary access controls may miss, such as an authorised government employee abusing privileges to share classified information. It also connected insider-threat research with scalable analysis of real online-community data.
misconceptions: ADAMS was not one specific anomaly-detection algorithm; it was a DARPA project containing multiple research efforts.
Wikipedia and Slashdot supplied research datasets for ADEN; they were not the project's only intended setting.
ADAMS was aimed at supporting counterintelligence operators, not at automatically declaring every unusual person malicious.
